Genetic testing prolong lives

By: Annalise Lubbe | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We travel to the heart of Namaqua to see how genetic research and clinical surveillance has prolonged the lives of potential cancer victims of the Cape’s most disadvantaged people.

Unique Selling Point:
In the mid 1980’s in the small town of Kommagas in the northern Cape a group of individuals were identified as having inherited colon cancer. A team of specialists found that they carried a mutation in a gene which results in colon, uterine, ovarian and other cancers. Those who carried the mutation developed cancers at a young age. An annual surveillance program was established in 19984 with the purpose of early detection and removal of any tissue that may become cancerous. Since then 400 known individuals in the Northern Cape who carried the mutation and were at a very high risk for development of cancers, have been helped, adding at least 20 years of life to those who joined the programme. Through genetic testing only targeted individuals who were at risk were then sent for colonoscopies. The colonoscopy in turn was the surveillance that contributed immensely to prolong life.


Summary:
In the heart of Namaqualand in the Northern Cape a team of medical specialists from Cape Town’s Groote Schuur hospital and University of the Cape have set up a base station. They are here in the little town of Garies for a two-day surveillance programme. In the heat of the summer sun, a group of people are already waiting anxiously for their annual check-up. Some have come from as far as Port Nolloth in the north, a three hour drive, to be checked for any possible cancers which run in their families.

The team consists of surgeons, anaesthetists, gynecologists, counselors, nurses and geneticists among them. Kitted out with the latest state-of-the-art medical equipment patients will be screened for cancers of the colon, uterine, ovarian and breast. The 50-strong support team are here to provide their expert services to individuals who have been identified with inherited cancers back in 1989 through the hard work of geneticist, Professor Raj Ramesar. Over the next two days more than 60 patients will be scanned for lesions that potentially could lead to cancer if not removed.

The success of the surveillance programme contributed to the breakthrough Prof Ramesar and his team had in 1998, ten years after his first field visit to identify the genetic defect which caused familial cancers. He traced the gene back to an individual who lived 500 years ago carrying the genetic defect that caused colon cancer. Studies revealed that in every family where this defect is present, 50% of the members would be at risk. Early detection and treatment would therefore be vital to prevent the cancer from killing half of each family carrying the gene.

The genetic results were shared with Professor Paul Greyling, Head of Gastroenterological Surgery at the Groote Schuur hospital, and his team who then put measures in place to assist the families with medical treatment offered in the annual field surveillance programme in the Northern Cape.


Further information:
In 1989 Professor Raj Ramesar set out to some remote parts in the northern Cape to conduct field research. His aim was to identify the genetic defect which causes familial cancers, i.g. cancers running in a family. At that stage the identification of the gene and genetic defect was a far cry from what it is today. His tireless work resulted in the identification of specific genetic defects in several South African families. There was an enormous value in this because of the involvement of the clinical surveillance team from the Departments of Medicine and Surgery who would benefit from his research once he identified the genetic lineages and those at risk of developing cancer. Individuals who were identified as having this cancer were then referred for colonoscopic surveillance. The field work involved taking the expert medical team into remote parts of the country where the identified individuals and their family members were tested and underwent treatment. Treatment involved a colonoscopy and removal of lesions before it turned into cancer. The fieldwork was laborious, time-consuming. It covered a vast terrain in the Western and Northern Cape provinces seeing many families on a once-a-year surveillance.

Whereas previously, all first and second degree blood relatives of an affected individual would be advised to undergo invasive colonoscopy procedure, the identification of a range of other genes and genetic defects has led to family-specific testing being developed in the last ten years. Professor Ramesar’s personal commitment has been to unearth the extensive genetic lineages in remote parts of the country, particularly the neglected Nama population of the Northern Cape.

Field visits involved the help of a translator and guide from the Nama community who would explain the purpose of the visit and the possible risks to family members of the individual who carried the mutation. Once they understood the benefits of early detection and treatment they were willing to be added to the programme. Over the last twenty years more than 400 individuals were identified as carrying the mutation and lesions removed in those family members at risk.

Prof Ramesar explained: “If I have colon cancer then my kids are all at 50% risk of getting this disease. My work has helped me to find the mutation and apply a quick genetic test which takes less than 2 hours in the lab with just a piece of DNA either from the mouth swab or from blood. So we are able to say exactly who is carrying the mutation. So the 50% of the individuals who are not carrying the mutation will be released from follow up.”

“Counselling forms an important part of the programme as many of the people are sceptical about being treated when they show no signs of being sick. But once they see the risk of getting the mutation from their infected family member, they are willing to go onto our register and see us for an annual check-up and removal of any tissue that might turn into cancer.”


In 2007 Professor Ramesar was nominated for the prestigious Alan Pfeifer Award based on his medical research among the remote communities in the Northern and Western Cape Provinces. This work has led to a highly effective intervention that has reduced the suffering and death due to cancers in these communities. His work has been exemplary in translating high technology genetic research into a rapid means for identifying those relatives in genetic lineages who are at highest risk by a relatively simple genetic test. Its translational success has been the significant reduction in disease burden families at highest risk, because of a personal commencement by Professor Ramesar to trace genetic lineages and to ensure information and genetic counselling, even in the remotest parts of the provinces. The genetic research, coupled to a clinical surveillance programme in the remote regions, is what has made the translation so successful. Professor Paul Goldberg of the Surgical Gastroenterology Unit at Groote Schuur Hospital and his team were the other important cogs in the wheel, responsible for the clinical surveillance programme in these remote parts.

The story:
We spend two days in Garies where we capture the tireless work of a dedicated team providing state-of-the-art medical surveillance to families who have been identified as carriers of the genetic cancer mutation. Interviews with key members of the medical surveillance team in Garies: Colorectal surgeons, Professor Paul Goldberg and Dr Adam Boutall; Prof Justiaan Swanevelder, anaesthetist; Dr Deon Lavine, physician and Gillian Dusterwald, genetic counsellor.

Our case studies will include two Rastafarian boys whose mother had the defect gene and are now on this programme to mitigate their risk of contracting the cancer. They live in a nearby village and have been on the programme for several years. Our second case study is family from Hondeklipbaai on the west Coast of Namaqua who have all tested positive for the defective gene which they inherited from their mother who died in her late fourties from colon cancer. Their daughters are now also on the surveillance programme to ensure that any potential polyps are removed before turning cancerous. The third case study is family from Garies. A mother with two boys, both positive, and one girl, negative. They are all on the surveillance programme for regular screening and removal of potentially cancerous lesions. In all three case studies, their livese have been prolonged with many years due to the early detention and treatment of the defective gene that is passed on from generation to generation.

Finally, we will pay a visit to the lab at the University of Cape Town where Prof Ramesar will share his genetic breakthrough story with us of how it changed the lives of the blood relatives of an infected individual through predictive testing.

Script:


Script: Genetic testing prolong lives
Duration: 10 minutes
Date: 26 November 2021

Link: We are on our way from Cape Town locked and loaded with camera gear and personal kit for a couple of nights. Our destination? Garies in Namaqualand where families have been devastated by colon and other cancers going back countless generations.

Lya Brandt: Cancer patient: As jy gedink het aan kanker (If you’ve thought about cancer,) of jy het dit net gehoor (or just heard about it,) dan het jy die dood gesien. (then you’ve seen death.)

Werner Carsten - Cancer patient: I lost my mom in 2012. She was diagnosed with colon cancer in 2011. Three months after that I was diagnosed.

Gericke Carsten - Cancer patient: I lost my father. I was only 10 years old so for me it was a different story. I always knew a dad that was sick.

V/O Namaqualand is a vast district with off the beaten track roads connecting families who live in this arid land. For the last thirty years, this region has been plagued by colon cancer claiming many lives. To shed light on why, our journey actually begins at the University of Cape Town with a geneticist who began asking questions many years ago. “Could it be in their DNA” he wondered? Determined to find out, Prof. Raj Ramesar found clues in the work of earlier doctors.

Derek Watts: Prof you are a young specialist and there was this dusty file, what was in there?

Prof. Raj Ramesar: Head of Human Genetics: University of Cape Town - Yah, there was this absolute treasure and this was very early work done by my predecessor, who in fact had heard of this condition, a form of inherited cancer, evidence by the fact there was several relatives working at a mine in Kleinzee.

V/O Kleinzee was not the only community affected. Ramesar found individuals from across Namaqualand being treated for colon cancer at Groote Schuur Hospital.

Prof. Raj Ramesar: What was hugely important is to do the research. So we gathered biological material, i.e. blood, and my work in the laboratory then was to try and figure out what is it that all affected individuals share.

Link: Prof. Ramesar’s research started in 1989 when he went to remote villages in the far corners of Namaqualand hoping to find the clue to the puzzle why so many families were battling with similar cancers.

V/O Ramesar suspected the problem might be in their genes - a mistake or misfiring within the molecules that make up DNA that were causing a mutation.

Prof. Raj Ramesar: So we would take the family history. Where did the disease come from? So perhaps his father had the disease. So with him having inherited the disease he had a 50% chance of passing it on to his kids.

LINK: Back in the lab at the university of Cape Town prof Ramasar was eager to find the answer but the breakthrough only came months later miles away in Chicago when he finally cracked the code.

V/O Ramesar was on a sabbatical in the U.S city working around the clock to find the answer.

Prof. Raj Ramesar: I remember it was a cold winter’s night when I found the genetic defect and it still sends shivers down my spine.

Derek Watts: Shivers down your spine.

Prof: Absolutely; I was so excited.

V/O What Ramesar found was a genetic defect present in all the individuals who carried the mutation, unique to South Africa, passed on from generation to generation.

Prof. Raj Ramesar: So in fact this mutation is more than a 1000 years old. What we know is this mutation arose here and it is prevalent here.

Derek Watts: It's homegrown.

Prof. Raj Ramesar: It's very much homegrown.

V/O Back in Garies, it’s late afternoon when we meet up with Lya Brandt (pronounced Lea), eager to share her story.

Lya Brandt - Cancer patient: Ek het groot geword in Paulshoek, (I grew up in Paulshoek..) in a matjieshuis gebly (in a ‘matjieshuis’.) Ons was a close familie. (We were a close family.)

V/O Lya took us back in time, to when Ramesar, accompanied by Sister Ursula Algar from Groote Schuur Hospital took blood samples to help track her family history. But before the test results were in Lya started experiencing stomach cramps.

Lya Brandt: Dit was eerstelik maandeliks (At first it was monthly...) en dit is later 2 dae uitmekaar uit (...then every second day.) maar dit is n pyn wat ek nie kon hanteer nie. (But, I couldn't handle the pain.)

V/O Lya was rushed to Groote Schuur hospital but it was too late. Her colon was riddled with cancer and had to be removed.

Lya Brand: Ja hulle het my hele dikderm verwyder (Yes, they removed my entire colon...) en het net twee stukkies gelos (only leaving a fraction.)

Derek Watts; I think Lea you’ve got the right spirit hey? Very positive.

Lya Brand: Ek is. Ek glo nie ek gaan weer kanker kry nie. (I am. I believe I am cured.)

V/O Lya is only one of over 500 individuals identified with this specific mutation that causes colon cancer. Multiply that by the 50% hereditary rate, and the numbers run into the thousands. Sister Algar’s mammoth task was to draw up a family tree going back generations.

Derek Watts: Sister we’ve got this scroll here it is almost like a family tree. How many years are we going back here?

Sister Ursula Algar - Co-ordinator Colorectal Family Cancer: Groote Schuur Hospital: So you are looking at least, if I can't get to it, one, two, three, four, five, six generations.

Derek Watts: Six generations.

Derek Watts: In the middle of this you have Lya and her children.

Sister Ursula Algar: Lya’s one of them. But she has been identified with the mutation which means her children are all 50% at risk and we tested all three of them, one isn’t the other two are.

V/O Lya’s one son, Augosto, and her daughter Bernice tested positive.

V/O Ramesar’s groundbreaking genetic discovery 3 decades ago led to a clinical surveillance programme rolled out in Namaqualand. High risk individuals were enrolled in the programme which involved annual screening at a rural clinic where they received sophisticated medical procedures by a team of specialists who came from hospitals across the country to offer their services. Prof Paul Goldberg has led the team for the past 27 years.

Derek Watts: Prof. so impressive this team coming together in this small community? It must take a lot of planning.

Prof. Paul Goldberg - Head Gastroenterological surgery: University of the Free State - It takes about a year. There is equipment that gets flown in from overseas particularly for the trip so the endoscopy equipment is actually brought in from all over the world. We have added more components. We have added breast screening. So the team has grown from 10 initially to about 50 that we are on now.

Derek Watts: It really is an amazing and heart-warming situation that these rural communities are getting the very best attention, the medical equipment.

Prof. Paul Goldberg: Absolutely. If you are going to have a colonoscopy in sa today. The place to have it is here in Garies.

LINK: For the next three days this clinic becomes a hive of activity as medical experts from around the country using the very latest equipment, carry out procedures for those families who are at high risk.

Derek Watts: Doctor what has it been like joining this team, for five years?

Dr Adam Boutall: Head of Colorectal Unit: Groote Schuur Hospital - It’s been a fantastic experience. Seeing patients again and again is a fantasticly rewarding experience because we really get to know the families and the people and you form a relationship with them. And they really appreciate what we are doing and we have a good time doing it.

UP SOUND

V/O Lya has not missed an annual check-up since they removed her colon. She is in good hands as Dr Adam Boutall picks up a tiny polyp which he removes with precision.

V/O We bumped into Werner and Gericke Cartsten in the clinic’s foyer. They’re from Aggenhuis, 200 km from Garies. They both inherited the mutation. Gericke, from her father who died when she was ten, and Werner, from his mother who passed away from colon cancer. Werner’s colon was removed the year before he joined the programme.

Werner Carsten: Cancer patient: Where I am from this local community, small communities, when you hear the word cancer its like a death penalty. We are doing this precaution because I want to live long and I can do it with the programme and by the will of God I can do it.

Gericke Carsten - Cancer patient: I think this programme makes a huge difference especially in our districts where there is nothing.

V/O The Carstens will have to remain in the programme, and their eleven year old daughter Wernice who carries the gene, will enter it when she turns 18.

Gericke Carsten: It's a lot of explaining to her at 11 to let her know that actually this feels bad now but it's for the good.

Up sound - Gericke in colonoscopy room going in for procedure

Derek Watts: It must be making a massive difference amongst the community?

Prof. Paul Goldberg: For those individuals who have the mutation and choose to enter the screening programme they get an additional 20 years at least of life. So instead of dying in their forties we get them up to 60 and beyond.

V/O When Ramesar and his team started their work 30 years ago, they could not have imagined the legacy their work would leave behind. The people of Namaqualand have been given a new lease on life and renewed hope that this generation’s children stand a better chance of beating an inherited cancer.

UP SOUND

V/O Before leaving, it was back to Lea’s house. Sister Algar was taking more blood and checking up on Lea after her recent procedure. As usual, Lya was full of beans.

Lya Brand: Ek is positief oor ons toekoms. (I am positive about the future.) Ek vertrou die here sal ons hierdeur help (I trust in the Lord to carry us through,) en dat ons anderkant alright sal uitkom. (and that we will be fine.)

UP SOUND Ursula saying goodbye

Promo one: 22 seconds
Lya Brand: Cancer patient: As jy gedink het aan kanker of jy het dit net gehoor, dan het jy die dood gesien.
V/O It was a cancer that took the lives of families for generations but after years of research it was traced to a genetic mutation, and now every year teams of medical experts descend on a clinic in Namaqualand to keep these cancers at bay.

Promo two: 22 seconds
V/O For decades families from Namaqualand have been plagued by certain cancers caused by a mutation they inherited, but now there is hope.
Prof Paul Goldberg: For those individuals who have the mutation and choose to enter the screening programme they get an additional 20 years at least of life. So instead of dying in their forties we get them up to 60 and beyond.

Promo three: 11 seconds
V/O Once a year this small clinic in Namaqualand turns into a state-of-the-art medical facility to help families keep a disease at bay they inherited from an individual centuries ago.

Sunday promo: 22 seconds
Prof Raj Ramesar: So we would take the family history. Where did the disease come from? So perhaps his father had the disease. So with him having inherited the disease he had a 50% chance of passing it on to his kids.
Derick Watts: After years of research it was traced to a genetic mutation and now every year teams of medical experts descend on the clinic to try and keep these cancers at bay.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 14 February 2022 Script: Script: Genetic testing prolong lives Duration: 10 minutes Date: 26 November 2021 Link: We are on our way from Cape Town locked and loaded with camera gear and personal kit for a couple of nights. Our destination? Garies in Namaqualand where families have been devastated by colon and other cancers going back countless generations. Lya Brandt: Cancer patient: As jy gedink het aan kanker (If you’ve thought about cancer,) of jy het dit net gehoor (or just heard about it,) dan het jy die dood gesien. (then you’ve seen death.) Werner Carsten - Cancer patient: I lost my mom in 2012. She was diagnosed with colon cancer in 2011. Three months after that I was diagnosed. Gericke Carsten - Cancer patient: I lost my father. I was only 10 years old so for me it was a different story. I always knew a dad that was sick. V/O Namaqualand is a vast district with off the beaten track roads connecting families who live in this arid land. For the last thirty years, this region has been plagued by colon cancer claiming many lives. To shed light on why, our journey actually begins at the University of Cape Town with a geneticist who began asking questions many years ago. “Could it be in their DNA” he wondered? Determined to find out, Prof. Raj Ramesar found clues in the work of earlier doctors. Derek Watts: Prof you are a young specialist and there was this dusty file, what was in there? Prof. Raj Ramesar: Head of Human Genetics: University of Cape Town - Yah, there was this absolute treasure and this was very early work done by my predecessor, who in fact had heard of this condition, a form of inherited cancer, evidence by the fact there was several relatives working at a mine in Kleinzee. V/O Kleinzee was not the only community affected. Ramesar found individuals from across Namaqualand being treated for colon cancer at Groote Schuur Hospital. Prof. Raj Ramesar: What was hugely important is to do the research. So we gathered biological material, i.e. blood, and my work in the laboratory then was to try and figure out what is it that all affected individuals share. Link: Prof. Ramesar’s research started in 1989 when he went to remote villages in the far corners of Namaqualand hoping to find the clue to the puzzle why so many families were battling with similar cancers. V/O Ramesar suspected the problem might be in their genes - a mistake or misfiring within the molecules that make up DNA that were causing a mutation. Prof. Raj Ramesar: So we would take the family history. Where did the disease come from? So perhaps his father had the disease. So with him having inherited the disease he had a 50% chance of passing it on to his kids. LINK: Back in the lab at the university of Cape Town prof Ramasar was eager to find the answer but the breakthrough only came months later miles away in Chicago when he finally cracked the code. V/O Ramesar was on a sabbatical in the U.S city working around the clock to find the answer. Prof. Raj Ramesar: I remember it was a cold winter’s night when I found the genetic defect and it still sends shivers down my spine. Derek Watts: Shivers down your spine. Prof: Absolutely; I was so excited. V/O What Ramesar found was a genetic defect present in all the individuals who carried the mutation, unique to South Africa, passed on from generation to generation. Prof. Raj Ramesar: So in fact this mutation is more than a 1000 years old. What we know is this mutation arose here and it is prevalent here. Derek Watts: It's homegrown. Prof. Raj Ramesar: It's very much homegrown. V/O Back in Garies, it’s late afternoon when we meet up with Lya Brandt (pronounced Lea), eager to share her story. Lya Brandt - Cancer patient: Ek het groot geword in Paulshoek, (I grew up in Paulshoek..) in a matjieshuis gebly (in a ‘matjieshuis’.) Ons was a close familie. (We were a close family.) V/O Lya took us back in time, to when Ramesar, accompanied by Sister Ursula Algar from Groote Schuur Hospital took blood samples to help track her family history. But before the test results were in Lya started experiencing stomach cramps. Lya Brandt: Dit was eerstelik maandeliks (At first it was monthly...) en dit is later 2 dae uitmekaar uit (...then every second day.) maar dit is n pyn wat ek nie kon hanteer nie. (But, I couldn't handle the pain.) V/O Lya was rushed to Groote Schuur hospital but it was too late. Her colon was riddled with cancer and had to be removed. Lya Brand: Ja hulle het my hele dikderm verwyder (Yes, they removed my entire colon...) en het net twee stukkies gelos (only leaving a fraction.) Derek Watts; I think Lea you’ve got the right spirit hey? Very positive. Lya Brand: Ek is. Ek glo nie ek gaan weer kanker kry nie. (I am. I believe I am cured.) V/O Lya is only one of over 500 individuals identified with this specific mutation that causes colon cancer. Multiply that by the 50% hereditary rate, and the numbers run into the thousands. Sister Algar’s mammoth task was to draw up a family tree going back generations. Derek Watts: Sister we’ve got this scroll here it is almost like a family tree. How many years are we going back here? Sister Ursula Algar - Co-ordinator Colorectal Family Cancer: Groote Schuur Hospital: So you are looking at least, if I can't get to it, one, two, three, four, five, six generations. Derek Watts: Six generations. Derek Watts: In the middle of this you have Lya and her children. Sister Ursula Algar: Lya’s one of them. But she has been identified with the mutation which means her children are all 50% at risk and we tested all three of them, one isn’t the other two are. V/O Lya’s one son, Augosto, and her daughter Bernice tested positive. V/O Ramesar’s groundbreaking genetic discovery 3 decades ago led to a clinical surveillance programme rolled out in Namaqualand. High risk individuals were enrolled in the programme which involved annual screening at a rural clinic where they received sophisticated medical procedures by a team of specialists who came from hospitals across the country to offer their services. Prof Paul Goldberg has led the team for the past 27 years. Derek Watts: Prof. so impressive this team coming together in this small community? It must take a lot of planning. Prof. Paul Goldberg - Head Gastroenterological surgery: University of the Free State - It takes about a year. There is equipment that gets flown in from overseas particularly for the trip so the endoscopy equipment is actually brought in from all over the world. We have added more components. We have added breast screening. So the team has grown from 10 initially to about 50 that we are on now. Derek Watts: It really is an amazing and heart-warming situation that these rural communities are getting the very best attention, the medical equipment. Prof. Paul Goldberg: Absolutely. If you are going to have a colonoscopy in sa today. The place to have it is here in Garies. LINK: For the next three days this clinic becomes a hive of activity as medical experts from around the country using the very latest equipment, carry out procedures for those families who are at high risk. Derek Watts: Doctor what has it been like joining this team, for five years? Dr Adam Boutall: Head of Colorectal Unit: Groote Schuur Hospital - It’s been a fantastic experience. Seeing patients again and again is a fantasticly rewarding experience because we really get to know the families and the people and you form a relationship with them. And they really appreciate what we are doing and we have a good time doing it. UP SOUND V/O Lya has not missed an annual check-up since they removed her colon. She is in good hands as Dr Adam Boutall picks up a tiny polyp which he removes with precision. V/O We bumped into Werner and Gericke Cartsten in the clinic’s foyer. They’re from Aggenhuis, 200 km from Garies. They both inherited the mutation. Gericke, from her father who died when she was ten, and Werner, from his mother who passed away from colon cancer. Werner’s colon was removed the year before he joined the programme. Werner Carsten: Cancer patient: Where I am from this local community, small communities, when you hear the word cancer its like a death penalty. We are doing this precaution because I want to live long and I can do it with the programme and by the will of God I can do it. Gericke Carsten - Cancer patient: I think this programme makes a huge difference especially in our districts where there is nothing. V/O The Carstens will have to remain in the programme, and their eleven year old daughter Wernice who carries the gene, will enter it when she turns 18. Gericke Carsten: It's a lot of explaining to her at 11 to let her know that actually this feels bad now but it's for the good. Up sound - Gericke in colonoscopy room going in for procedure Derek Watts: It must be making a massive difference amongst the community? Prof. Paul Goldberg: For those individuals who have the mutation and choose to enter the screening programme they get an additional 20 years at least of life. So instead of dying in their forties we get them up to 60 and beyond. V/O When Ramesar and his team started their work 30 years ago, they could not have imagined the legacy their work would leave behind. The people of Namaqualand have been given a new lease on life and renewed hope that this generation’s children stand a better chance of beating an inherited cancer. UP SOUND V/O Before leaving, it was back to Lea’s house. Sister Algar was taking more blood and checking up on Lea after her recent procedure. As usual, Lya was full of beans. Lya Brand: Ek is positief oor ons toekoms. (I am positive about the future.) Ek vertrou die here sal ons hierdeur help (I trust in the Lord to carry us through,) en dat ons anderkant alright sal uitkom. (and that we will be fine.) UP SOUND Ursula saying goodbye ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo one: 22 seconds Lya Brand: Cancer patient: As jy gedink het aan kanker of jy het dit net gehoor, dan het jy die dood gesien. V/O It was a cancer that took the lives of families for generations but after years of research it was traced to a genetic mutation, and now every year teams of medical experts descend on a clinic in Namaqualand to keep these cancers at bay. Promo two: 22 seconds V/O For decades families from Namaqualand have been plagued by certain cancers caused by a mutation they inherited, but now there is hope. Prof Paul Goldberg: For those individuals who have the mutation and choose to enter the screening programme they get an additional 20 years at least of life. So instead of dying in their forties we get them up to 60 and beyond. Promo three: 11 seconds V/O Once a year this small clinic in Namaqualand turns into a state-of-the-art medical facility to help families keep a disease at bay they inherited from an individual centuries ago. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We travel to the heart of Namaqua to see how genetic research and clinical surveillance has prolonged the lives of potential cancer victims of the Cape’s most disadvantaged people.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the mid 1980’s in the small town of Kommagas in the northern Cape a group of individuals were identified as having inherited colon cancer. A team of specialists found that they carried a mutation in a gene which results in colon, uterine, ovarian and other cancers. Those who carried the mutation developed cancers at a young age. An annual surveillance program was established in 19984 with the purpose of early detection and removal of any tissue that may become cancerous. Since then 400 known individuals in the Northern Cape who carried the mutation and were at a very high risk for development of cancers, have been helped, adding at least 20 years of life to those who joined the programme. Through genetic testing only targeted individuals who were at risk were then sent for colonoscopies. The colonoscopy in turn was the surveillance that contributed immensely to prolong life.
metadata.Summary: In the heart of Namaqualand in the Northern Cape a team of medical specialists from Cape Town’s Groote Schuur hospital and University of the Cape have set up a base station. They are here in the little town of Garies for a two-day surveillance programme. In the heat of the summer sun, a group of people are already waiting anxiously for their annual check-up. Some have come from as far as Port Nolloth in the north, a three hour drive, to be checked for any possible cancers which run in their families. The team consists of surgeons, anaesthetists, gynecologists, counselors, nurses and geneticists among them. Kitted out with the latest state-of-the-art medical equipment patients will be screened for cancers of the colon, uterine, ovarian and breast. The 50-strong support team are here to provide their expert services to individuals who have been identified with inherited cancers back in 1989 through the hard work of geneticist, Professor Raj Ramesar. Over the next two days more than 60 patients will be scanned for lesions that potentially could lead to cancer if not removed. The success of the surveillance programme contributed to the breakthrough Prof Ramesar and his team had in 1998, ten years after his first field visit to identify the genetic defect which caused familial cancers. He traced the gene back to an individual who lived 500 years ago carrying the genetic defect that caused colon cancer. Studies revealed that in every family where this defect is present, 50% of the members would be at risk. Early detection and treatment would therefore be vital to prevent the cancer from killing half of each family carrying the gene. The genetic results were shared with Professor Paul Greyling, Head of Gastroenterological Surgery at the Groote Schuur hospital, and his team who then put measures in place to assist the families with medical treatment offered in the annual field surveillance programme in the Northern Cape.
metadata.Further information: In 1989 Professor Raj Ramesar set out to some remote parts in the northern Cape to conduct field research. His aim was to identify the genetic defect which causes familial cancers, i.g. cancers running in a family. At that stage the identification of the gene and genetic defect was a far cry from what it is today. His tireless work resulted in the identification of specific genetic defects in several South African families. There was an enormous value in this because of the involvement of the clinical surveillance team from the Departments of Medicine and Surgery who would benefit from his research once he identified the genetic lineages and those at risk of developing cancer. Individuals who were identified as having this cancer were then referred for colonoscopic surveillance. The field work involved taking the expert medical team into remote parts of the country where the identified individuals and their family members were tested and underwent treatment. Treatment involved a colonoscopy and removal of lesions before it turned into cancer. The fieldwork was laborious, time-consuming. It covered a vast terrain in the Western and Northern Cape provinces seeing many families on a once-a-year surveillance. Whereas previously, all first and second degree blood relatives of an affected individual would be advised to undergo invasive colonoscopy procedure, the identification of a range of other genes and genetic defects has led to family-specific testing being developed in the last ten years. Professor Ramesar’s personal commitment has been to unearth the extensive genetic lineages in remote parts of the country, particularly the neglected Nama population of the Northern Cape. Field visits involved the help of a translator and guide from the Nama community who would explain the purpose of the visit and the possible risks to family members of the individual who carried the mutation. Once they understood the benefits of early detection and treatment they were willing to be added to the programme. Over the last twenty years more than 400 individuals were identified as carrying the mutation and lesions removed in those family members at risk. Prof Ramesar explained: “If I have colon cancer then my kids are all at 50% risk of getting this disease. My work has helped me to find the mutation and apply a quick genetic test which takes less than 2 hours in the lab with just a piece of DNA either from the mouth swab or from blood. So we are able to say exactly who is carrying the mutation. So the 50% of the individuals who are not carrying the mutation will be released from follow up.” “Counselling forms an important part of the programme as many of the people are sceptical about being treated when they show no signs of being sick. But once they see the risk of getting the mutation from their infected family member, they are willing to go onto our register and see us for an annual check-up and removal of any tissue that might turn into cancer.” In 2007 Professor Ramesar was nominated for the prestigious Alan Pfeifer Award based on his medical research among the remote communities in the Northern and Western Cape Provinces. This work has led to a highly effective intervention that has reduced the suffering and death due to cancers in these communities. His work has been exemplary in translating high technology genetic research into a rapid means for identifying those relatives in genetic lineages who are at highest risk by a relatively simple genetic test. Its translational success has been the significant reduction in disease burden families at highest risk, because of a personal commencement by Professor Ramesar to trace genetic lineages and to ensure information and genetic counselling, even in the remotest parts of the provinces. The genetic research, coupled to a clinical surveillance programme in the remote regions, is what has made the translation so successful. Professor Paul Goldberg of the Surgical Gastroenterology Unit at Groote Schuur Hospital and his team were the other important cogs in the wheel, responsible for the clinical surveillance programme in these remote parts. The story: We spend two days in Garies where we capture the tireless work of a dedicated team providing state-of-the-art medical surveillance to families who have been identified as carriers of the genetic cancer mutation. Interviews with key members of the medical surveillance team in Garies: Colorectal surgeons, Professor Paul Goldberg and Dr Adam Boutall; Prof Justiaan Swanevelder, anaesthetist; Dr Deon Lavine, physician and Gillian Dusterwald, genetic counsellor. Our case studies will include two Rastafarian boys whose mother had the defect gene and are now on this programme to mitigate their risk of contracting the cancer. They live in a nearby village and have been on the programme for several years. Our second case study is family from Hondeklipbaai on the west Coast of Namaqua who have all tested positive for the defective gene which they inherited from their mother who died in her late fourties from colon cancer. Their daughters are now also on the surveillance programme to ensure that any potential polyps are removed before turning cancerous. The third case study is family from Garies. A mother with two boys, both positive, and one girl, negative. They are all on the surveillance programme for regular screening and removal of potentially cancerous lesions. In all three case studies, their livese have been prolonged with many years due to the early detention and treatment of the defective gene that is passed on from generation to generation. Finally, we will pay a visit to the lab at the University of Cape Town where Prof Ramesar will share his genetic breakthrough story with us of how it changed the lives of the blood relatives of an infected individual through predictive testing. ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
